 Live Global Flood Map
 This map combines two complementary sources of information: recent flood events reported by GDACS , marked with the 🌊 symbol, and areas detected as flooded by satellite . Permanent water and areas where satellite observations are insufficient are hidden to make recent flood signals easier to identify.
 The satellite layer uses NASA's global VIIRS flood product. The two-day composite combines observations from the displayed date and the previous day. At low zoom levels, a global overview makes large patterns easier to locate; from zoom level 6 onward, higher-resolution satellite tiles aligned with the map are used.
 Map updated 2026-10-24 10:31 UTC — 2-day observations through 2026-10-23 
 Map layers: 
 Satellite-detected flooded areas 
 🌊 Recent flood events reported by GDACS 
 Dark blue: areas where flooding was detected by VIIRS satellite observations. Their apparent width on screen must not be used to measure the true flooded area.
🌊: flood event reported by GDACS; the marker indicates the affected region approximately.
Data: NASA EOSDIS / LANCE / GIBS (VIIRS_Combined_Flood_2-Day).
Recent events: Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS).
Basemap: OpenFreeMap / OpenMapTiles, data © OpenStreetMap contributors. Land/sea filtering: OSM Land Mask via NASA GIBS. 
 How to Interpret the Global Flood Map
 The 🌊 symbols identify recent flood events reported by GDACS . They help locate regions that may deserve closer inspection: clicking a marker zooms to the area, while the satellite pixels show surfaces actually detected as flooded. The marker position is only an approximate event location and does not represent the exact footprint of the inundation.
 What information does GDACS provide? 
Depending on the information available for each event, the popup can show the affected country and region , the event period , the GDACS alert level (green, orange or red), and human-impact data such as deaths, displaced people and, when available, people affected. GDACS may also report damaged homes and specific locations mentioned in its impact assessment.
For floods, the GDACS alert level takes into account factors including deaths and displaced people. These figures reflect information available at the time of the assessment and can be incomplete or revised as an event develops; missing values are therefore not displayed.
 Important interpretation note: seeing only a few dark-blue areas does not necessarily mean there are few floods worldwide. VIIRS is an optical instrument: clouds, vegetation, shadows, snow and gaps in coverage can hide some floods. The displayed two-day product combines the selected date with the previous day, so a dark-blue area may have been observed on either day.
 At low zoom levels, very small detections are deliberately enlarged slightly so they remain visible. From zoom level 6 onward, the map uses higher-resolution satellite tiles . At zoom levels 6 to 8, a small cartographic halo helps tiny clusters remain visible; this is only a visual aid and does not extend the real flooded area. A land/sea mask with a small coastal margin removes detections clearly offshore, and very small pixel clusters are filtered to reduce some artefacts. These treatments improve readability but must not be used to measure the actual flooded surface area.
